newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - New charges to delay Nomura punishment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - New charges to delay Nomura punishment.

text.p: Fresh allegations that a former Nomura Securities president made a huge payoff to a racketeer will likely delay a decision on administrative penalties against the brokerage, industry sources said on Friday.
And the longer the wait for a decision, the greater the damage to Nomura's bottom line, already dented by client defections as the high-profile scandal unfolds.

Tokyo prosecutors on Thursday charged former Nomura Securities Co Ltd president Hideo Sakamaki, who resigned over the scandal in March, with violating the Commercial Code by had by paying 49.73 million yen ($440,000) to "sokaiya" racketeer Ryuichi Koike between January 31 and June 15, 1995.

That indictment was widely anticipated. But in another blow to the brokerage, prosecutors served new arrest warrants on Sakamaki and two other former Nomura executives alleging the three conspired to pay 320 million yen ($2.80 million) in cash to Koike around March 24, 1995.
Prosecutors said the alleged payoff was aimed at ensuring the brokerage's June shareholders meeting went without a hitch.

The scandal has already led to more than a dozen arrests including executives from Nomura and from one of Japan's biggest banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd and worries persist that other financial firms will be entangled.
Nomura -- now entangled in its second scandal in six years -- has been indicted for illegally compensating a company owned by Koike's brother for trading losses.
Payoffs to sokaiya, who extort money by threatening to disrupt shareholders meetings, have been illegal since 1982 but firms have found it tough to cut their ties to the underworld.
A Nomura spokesman said on Friday that the brokerage would start an internal investigation into how Sakamaki obtained the 320 million yen ($2.80 million) to pay the racketeer.
If any illegal deals are uncovered, Nomura may take legal actions against Sakamaki depending on the outcome of prosecutors' probe, the spokesman added.
Experts had expected Sakamaki's indictment to clear the way for a decision on Nomura's penalties, which could include the suspension of some of its business for up to six months.

But financial authorities are unlikely to move until prosecutors, who on Friday raided a Nomura affiliate, have finished their probe -- and that could take at least until late next month, a government source said.

Further delay would erode Nomura's earnings. Whether the nation's biggest brokerage posts a profit in the current business year to next March depends on when the penalties are unveiled as well as how severe they are, analysts said.
Clients are already shunning the brokerage and it has been suspended from underwriting government and government-backed bonds due to the scandal.
If the suspension lasts into the second half of 1997/98, it might be difficult for Nomura to stay in the black this business year, some analysts said.

Still, many in the industry expect Nomura to maintain its top status in Japan's securities industry. "The scandal is unlikely to vitally hurt Nomura's financial strength. Nomura is the only Japanese brokerage which can compete with foreign rivals in the Big Bang deregulations," one analyst said.

In a sign, meanwhile, that the early 1990's brokerage scandal still haunts the industry, a Japanese newspaper on Friday reported that Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd had allegedly engaged in questionable deals worth some 36.6 billion yen with Tokyu Department Store Co Ltd between 1987 and 1992.
A Yamaichi spokesman said the brokerage could not confirm the report and would make no comment.
